screens.title: Understanding the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will make the Single Responsibility Principle concrete. SRP says a class should have only one reason to change. That phrasing is deceptively simple. It asks you to think in terms of responsibilities and causes of change, not in terms of method counts or line counts. You will learn how to spot when a class accumulates unrelated duties, how to decide what a single responsibility really is, and how to refactor practical Java examples so each class changes for one reason only. We'll use the User and ReportGenerator examples to show before and after states, and you'll practice a hands-on refactor with an Invoice example. Along the way we'll cover common mistakes teams make when they conflate persistence, presentation, validation, and notification. By the end you'll be able to explain SRP, point to concrete responsibilities in a class, and propose a minimal set of focused classes that follow SRP. Think about the last time you modified a class for two different reasons — that is the smell SRP helps you avoid. Ready to explore why smaller, focused classes help your code evolve more safely?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Understanding SRP
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Single Responsibility Principle

Learn to recognize when a class has multiple reasons to change and how to reorganize code so each class has a single, cohesive responsibility.

SRP focuses on causes of change. If different stakeholders or system changes would drive distinct edits, that indicates separate responsibilities. This lesson uses concrete Java examples and a hands-on refactor to make SRP practical.
Why it matters: smaller classes localize change, simplify tests, and reduce unintended coupling between unrelated behaviors like persistence, formatting, and notifications.
Explore Key Topics
Definition
What 'one reason to change' really means for classes and methods.
Violations & Examples
ReportGenerator and User examples that mix generation, persistence, and notification.
Refactoring Steps
Extract classes, inject dependencies, and keep behavior focused and testable.
Visual Concept
Before: One class, many reasons
After: Focused, single-responsibility classes
Quick Map
D
Data model: represents the object's fields and invariants.
V
Validation: rules that govern correctness of data.
I
Integration: persistence, email, printing are separate concerns to extract.
Notice how each colored badge hints at a distinct reason your class might change.

screens.title: What SRP Means: 'One Reason to Change'
screens.narratorSegment: Start by clarifying the phrase 'one reason to change.' A reason is an external driver that, if it evolves, will require edits to a class. That driver could be a change in technology, a business rule, a user-interface requirement, or an integration contract. The key claim is that a class should group behavior that changes together. If two behaviors have different causes for change, they should not live in the same class because a change in one domain will cause unrelated edits in the other. Consider a User class. Storage changes, UI formatting changes, validation changes, and email-sending changes are distinct drivers. If the class contains code for all of those, a change to the email provider forces edits unrelated to the user data model. A common misconception is to equate SRP with 'one method per class' or 'small classes only.' SRP allows many methods as long as they all support the single responsibility. Another misconception is to treat 'managing users' as a single responsibility — but persistence, validation, and notifications are separate reasons to change. A practical naming test helps: name the single reason a class should change. If you cannot name one concise reason, the class likely needs refactoring. To close, practice naming reasons for change when you read code; that naming is the most reliable SRP heuristic.

keyIdea.title: SRP definition
keyIdea.text: Group behaviors that change together. If two behaviors change for different reasons, extract them into separate classes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › SRP: One Reason
Definition

A "reason to change" is any driver that would cause you to edit a class. Drivers include technology choices, business rules, UI formats, and integration contracts. SRP asks that a class contain only behaviors tied to a single such driver.

Analogy
Think of a team chart: one person should own one role. If one person handles payroll and hiring, changes to payroll rules disturb hiring work.
Common misconception
SRP is not 'one method per class.' A class can have many methods that together serve the single responsibility.
Key Takeaway

Name the single reason a class should change. If you can name only one, it likely follows SRP.

Worked example — User class drivers
  • Storage changes: switching database types.
  • Validation rules: password complexity or address validation changes.
  • Presentation: how the user is rendered for the UI.
  • Notification: welcome email or password reset flows.
If the User class contains code for all four, any change among them forces edits across unrelated behavior — that is the smell of SRP violation.
Check your understanding
Try naming the single reason to change for a class you know. If you struggle, identify two behaviors that could be extracted.

screens.title: Identifying Responsibilities — A Practical Heuristic
screens.narratorSegment: To find responsibilities in an existing class, use a simple heuristic: list the external events that would cause this class to change. External events can be business rule updates, UI redesigns, library upgrades, or infrastructure shifts. For each method or block of code, ask: if this requirement changes, will other parts of the class need changing too? If not, the code likely belongs elsewhere. A step-by-step approach helps. First, enumerate methods and features. Second, for each feature name the reason it exists — persistence, formatting, calculation, notification. Third, cluster features by shared reasons and check whether those clusters align with class boundaries. Fourth, consider moving each cluster into its own class with a focused name like PdfReportGenerator or InvoicePrinter. A common pitfall is to treat helper utilities as part of the same responsibility simply because they are convenient. Resist this convenience. Focused classes reduce test setup and make expectations explicit. A short example: an Order class with methods to calculate tax, print invoices, and persist to the database should be split because tax rules, printing templates, and persistence strategies change for different reasons. End with a practical question: when you next review code, can you list the reasons each class might change?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Identifying Responsibilities
Step-by-step
  1. List methods and features in the class.
  2. For each, name the reason it exists (persistence, formatting, notification, calculation).
  3. Group methods that share the same reason to change.
  4. Extract each group into a well-named class and inject dependencies where needed.
Pitfall to avoid
Do not keep helper logic in the same class just because it’s convenient. Convenience creates hidden coupling and makes isolated tests harder.
Worked mini-scenario
Imagine an Order class with calculateTax(), save(), and printInvoice(). Ask: would a tax rule change affect how we save the order? No. Would a new printer template affect tax calculation? No. So tax calculation, persistence, and printing are separate responsibilities and should be separated into dedicated classes.
Pro tip

Use short, descriptive names for extracted classes that reveal the single responsibility, such as TaxCalculator, OrderRepository, or InvoicePrinter.

screens.title: User Class Example: Multiple Reasons to Change
screens.narratorSegment: The User class is a helpful thought experiment because it naturally touches several domains. The data representation holds fields such as username and email. Validation enforces rules such as password complexity. Persistence saves and loads users from storage. Presentation shapes how user data appears in the UI. And notification sends welcome or password-reset messages. These are distinct reasons to change: a new database vendor affects persistence code; a new password policy affects validation; a UI redesign affects presentation code; a change in the email provider affects notification logic. When all of these behaviors live in one class, any of these independent changes produces edits across unrelated behavior and increases the risk of regressions. A common misinterpretation is to keep persistence methods near the data because they seem closely related. But persistence often changes for infrastructure reasons that have nothing to do with domain invariants; separating persistence into a repository or data-access class keeps the domain model stable. To practice, inspect a User class and label each method with the single reason it would change. If you find more than one label, plan an extraction to restore SRP.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › User Class Example
Responsibilities often hidden in User
  • Data model: username, email, password hash.
  • Validation: password rules and input checks.
  • Persistence: save and load from database.
  • Presentation: formatting for views and APIs.
  • Notification: email or SMS messages.
Misconception
Keeping persistence and domain logic together is not always wrong, but when persistence changes independently, it becomes a separate reason to change and should be extracted.
Practical exercise
Open a User class and annotate each method with its reason to change. If you assign more than one reason inside the same class, plan to extract at least one responsibility into a new class with a clear name.
Common mistake

Allowing convenience to guide design. Adding a quick print or email function into a domain class invites unrelated changes later.

screens.title: ReportGenerator: The SRP Violator (Before)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine the ReportGenerator example to see SRP violations in code. The class handles deciding format, generating PDF and CSV content, saving to a file system, and emailing the report. Each responsibility is a potential independent cause of change: adding an H T M L format, replacing the PDF library, moving storage to cloud, or switching the email provider. When these concerns share a class, a fix for one area risks breaking others. Reading the code, identify responsibilities: format selection and generation, file input and output, and email sending. A good test is to ask: could I test PDF generation without touching email or file input and output? In the current design you cannot, making unit tests brittle and slow. The corrective pattern extracts classes such as PdfReportGenerator, CsvReportGenerator, ReportSaver, and ReportEmailer. Each becomes independently testable and replaceable. Below is the original ReportGenerator code so you can spot the multiple responsibilities visually and prepare for the split. ReportGenerator: The SRP Violator (Before) means reportgenerator mixes multiple responsibilities — each is a separate reason the class would change.. In practical terms, a single class mixing generation, persistence, and notification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › ReportGenerator — Before
Original Java snippet
public class ReportGenerator {
    public void generateReport(String data, String format) {
        if ("PDF".equals(format)) {
            generatePdfReport(data);
        } else if ("CSV".equals(format)) {
            generateCsvReport(data);
        } else {
            System.out.println("Unsupported report format.");
        }
    }

    private void generatePdfReport(String data) {
        System.out.println("Generating PDF report with data: " + data);
        // Complex PDF generation logic
    }

    private void generateCsvReport(String data) {
        System.out.println("Generating CSV report with data: " + data);
        // Complex CSV generation logic
    }

    public void saveReport(String reportContent, String filePath) {
        System.out.println("Saving report to: " + filePath);
        // File I/O logic
    }

    public void emailReport(String reportContent, String recipient) {
        System.out.println("Emailing report to: " + recipient);
        // Email sending logic
    }
}
Responsibilities to extract
  • Format selection and report generation (PDF, CSV).
  • PDF-specific generation logic that depends on a library.
  • CSV generation implementation.
  • Persistence: saving files.
  • Notification: emailing reports.
Why this is hard to test

Unit tests cannot isolate generation from file or email behavior, so tests become integration-style and brittle. Extraction enables small focused tests.

screens.title: ReportGenerator — After: Split Responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: A practical refactor decomposes the original ReportGenerator into focused classes. Each new class addresses a single reason to change. PdfReportGenerator owns PDF creation and can change if the PDF library changes. CsvReportGenerator owns CSV creation and can be replaced independently. ReportSaver handles persistence, and ReportEmailer handles notifications. Consumers orchestrate these classes rather than embedding all logic in one class. This approach makes each class independently testable: you can unit-test PdfReportGenerator for layout and content without touching storage or email. It reduces coupling because changes to the email provider only require changes in ReportEmailer. It also clarifies intent through class names, which improves readability for new team members. A common pitfall while extracting is moving too quickly and copying code without creating shared abstractions where appropriate. Aim for small, well-named classes and introduce an interface only when needed for multiple implementations. The transformation keeps external behavior the same but moves implementation responsibilities into focused, replaceable components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › ReportGenerator — After
After: Extracted classes
PdfReportGenerator — owns PDF creation and layout; changes when PDF library or format changes.
CsvReportGenerator — owns CSV generation details.
ReportSaver — handles persistence; replaceable for cloud or file-system storage.
ReportEmailer — sends report via email; isolated from content generation.
Composition example
A ReportService coordinates generators and services: it receives data, delegates generation to the appropriate generator, then calls ReportSaver or ReportEmailer as required. Each delegate can be tested and maintained independently.
Refactoring note
Extract first, then introduce interfaces only when you need multiple interchangeable implementations. Avoid premature abstraction.

screens.narratorSegment: Before refactoring, a single ReportGenerator class directly depends on PDF libraries, file input and output APIs, and mailing libraries. That tight coupling means any change in those libraries could force edits across unrelated logic. After refactoring, each focused class holds only the dependencies it needs: PdfReportGenerator depends on the PDF library, ReportSaver depends on storage APIs, ReportEmailer depends on the mail provider. This change reduces the blast radius of modifications and allows teams to upgrade or replace one area without risking others. It also creates clearer test boundaries: tests for PdfReportGenerator mock only the PDF output, and tests for ReportSaver focus on storage behavior. A common mistake is over-extracting and scattering related logic across too many tiny classes, which increases indirection. The correct balance keeps cohesion high in each class and coupling low between classes. Think of dependencies as contracts: each class promises to do one job and requires only the APIs to fulfill it. That explicitness simplifies maintenance and future changes. Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Dependency Architecture
Before
ReportGenerator directly calls PDF library, file system, and email provider. All concerns live in one place, so changing one external API requires touching the class that also handles generation.
Risk

High coupling increases the risk of regressions and makes upgrades costly.

After
PdfReportGenerator, CsvReportGenerator, ReportSaver, and ReportEmailer each hold only the dependencies they require. A change in the email provider touches only ReportEmailer.
Benefit

Reduced blast radius for changes and simpler, focused tests for each class.

screens.title: Refactoring Steps to Enforce SRP
screens.narratorSegment: A repeatable refactoring sequence helps you safely split responsibilities. Step one: identify the responsibilities by naming reasons to change for each method. Step two: pick one responsibility to extract first — choose the one with the clearest boundary or the largest pain point in tests. Step three: create a new class with a focused name that reflects the responsibility, and move the relevant methods and any required data. Step four: replace direct calls to side effects with dependency injection so callers receive the new class via constructor or factory. Step five: write unit tests for the new class and change existing tests to use test doubles where appropriate. Step six: remove the extracted behavior from the original class and confirm its remaining responsibility is cohesive. Finally, run integration tests to ensure behavior is preserved. A common error is extracting without writing tests — this increases risk. Always secure behavior with tests before and after the change. This incremental approach makes SRP practical even in a large, working codebase. Starter code (excerpt)
public class Invoice {
    private List items;
    private double taxRate;

    public Invoice(double taxRate) {

        this.taxRate = taxRate;

    public double calculateTotal() {

screens.title: Why SRP Improves Code Quality
screens.narratorSegment: Applying SRP yields measurable improvements in how your codebase evolves. Maintainability rises because changes are localized: when a requirement evolves, only the class representing that responsibility changes. Testability improves because classes have narrow scope and can be tested without large setup or many mocks. Reusability increases since focused classes like PdfGenerator can be reused by different parts of the system. Readability improves because class names and method lists clearly express intent. Coupling decreases because unrelated dependencies move to the classes that need them. Consider a scenario where the email provider changes: with SRP, only the EmailSender needs modification and tests, rather than multiple classes scattered across the codebase. A misconception is that SRP produces too many tiny classes; the right balance is high cohesion within each class and low coupling across classes. Finally, SRP supports incremental refactoring: small extractions make future changes safer and faster. As you adopt SRP, measure improvement by tracking how often a single change touches multiple classes — that frequency should decrease. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will make the Single Responsibility Principle concrete. SRP says a class should have only one reason to change. That phrasing is deceptively simple. It asks you to think in terms of responsibilities and causes of change, not in terms of method counts or line counts. You will learn how to spot when a class accumulates unrelated duties, how to decide what a single responsibility really is, and how to refactor practical Java examples so each class changes for one reason only. We'll use the User and ReportGenerator examples to show before and after states, and you'll practice a hands-on refactor with an Invoice example. Along the way we'll cover common mistakes teams make when they conflate persistence, presentation, validation, and notification. By the end you'll be able to explain SRP, point to concrete responsibilities in a class, and propose a minimal set of focused classes that follow SRP. Think about the last time you modified a class for two different reasons — that is the smell SRP helps you avoid. Ready to explore why smaller, focused classes help your code evolve more safely?

These objectives focus your practice so you can apply SRP in real code. First, you will be able to state SRP precisely as a rule about reasons to change, not about method counts. Second, you will learn to identify distinct responsibilities by asking what external events or requirement changes would force edits to a class. Third, you will recognize common violations by studying practical Java examples where generation, saving, and notification are mixed. Fourth, you will explain the benefits of SRP for maintainability, testability, and reduced coupling. Each objective pairs a clear skill with a short reason why it matters: defining SRP prevents misapplied rules, identifying responsibilities supports targeted refactors, reading examples builds diagnostic skill, and describing benefits helps you persuade team members to adopt the change. As you work through the examples and the hands-on refactor, test your understanding by naming the single reason for change for each class you inspect. That naming exercise is the simplest litmus test of SRP mastery.

These practice-focused objectives help you turn SRP from rule to habit. You will practice naming the single reason a class would change, then extract the behavior that does not share that reason. You'll read small Java examples and identify the boundaries between data representation, persistence, presentation, and notification. The chapter includes a hands-on refactor of an Invoice class: you'll move printing into an InvoicePrinter and confirm the Invoice class only calculates amounts. You'll also practice writing focused unit tests for each extracted class. Finally, you'll learn short heuristics to guide code review conversations: ask whether two different changes would touch the same class, and if the answer is yes, consider extraction. These heuristics are quick and practical and help teams avoid the slow drift toward multi-responsibility classes that become costly over time.

Start by clarifying the phrase 'one reason to change.' A reason is an external driver that, if it evolves, will require edits to a class. That driver could be a change in technology, a business rule, a user-interface requirement, or an integration contract. The key claim is that a class should group behavior that changes together. If two behaviors have different causes for change, they should not live in the same class because a change in one domain will cause unrelated edits in the other. Consider a User class. Storage changes, UI formatting changes, validation changes, and email-sending changes are distinct drivers. If the class contains code for all of those, a change to the email provider forces edits unrelated to the user data model. A common misconception is to equate SRP with 'one method per class' or 'small classes only.' SRP allows many methods as long as they all support the single responsibility. Another misconception is to treat 'managing users' as a single responsibility — but persistence, validation, and notifications are separate reasons to change. A practical naming test helps: name the single reason a class should change. If you cannot name one concise reason, the class likely needs refactoring. To close, practice naming reasons for change when you read code; that naming is the most reliable SRP heuristic.

To find responsibilities in an existing class, use a simple heuristic: list the external events that would cause this class to change. External events can be business rule updates, UI redesigns, library upgrades, or infrastructure shifts. For each method or block of code, ask: if this requirement changes, will other parts of the class need changing too? If not, the code likely belongs elsewhere. A step-by-step approach helps. First, enumerate methods and features. Second, for each feature name the reason it exists — persistence, formatting, calculation, notification. Third, cluster features by shared reasons and check whether those clusters align with class boundaries. Fourth, consider moving each cluster into its own class with a focused name like PdfReportGenerator or InvoicePrinter. A common pitfall is to treat helper utilities as part of the same responsibility simply because they are convenient. Resist this convenience. Focused classes reduce test setup and make expectations explicit. A short example: an Order class with methods to calculate tax, print invoices, and persist to the database should be split because tax rules, printing templates, and persistence strategies change for different reasons. End with a practical question: when you next review code, can you list the reasons each class might change?

The User class is a helpful thought experiment because it naturally touches several domains. The data representation holds fields such as username and email. Validation enforces rules such as password complexity. Persistence saves and loads users from storage. Presentation shapes how user data appears in the UI. And notification sends welcome or password-reset messages. These are distinct reasons to change: a new database vendor affects persistence code; a new password policy affects validation; a UI redesign affects presentation code; a change in the email provider affects notification logic. When all of these behaviors live in one class, any of these independent changes produces edits across unrelated behavior and increases the risk of regressions. A common misinterpretation is to keep persistence methods near the data because they seem closely related. But persistence often changes for infrastructure reasons that have nothing to do with domain invariants; separating persistence into a repository or data-access class keeps the domain model stable. To practice, inspect a User class and label each method with the single reason it would change. If you find more than one label, plan an extraction to restore SRP.

Let's examine the ReportGenerator example to see SRP violations in code. The class handles deciding format, generating PDF and CSV content, saving to a file system, and emailing the report. Each responsibility is a potential independent cause of change: adding an H T M L format, replacing the PDF library, moving storage to cloud, or switching the email provider. When these concerns share a class, a fix for one area risks breaking others. Reading the code, identify responsibilities: format selection and generation, file input and output, and email sending. A good test is to ask: could I test PDF generation without touching email or file input and output? In the current design you cannot, making unit tests brittle and slow. The corrective pattern extracts classes such as PdfReportGenerator, CsvReportGenerator, ReportSaver, and ReportEmailer. Each becomes independently testable and replaceable. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

PdfReportGenerator owns PDF creation and can change if the PDF library changes. CsvReportGenerator owns CSV creation and can be replaced independently. ReportSaver handles persistence, and ReportEmailer handles notifications. Consumers orchestrate these classes rather than embedding all logic in one class. This approach makes each class independently testable: you can unit-test PdfReportGenerator for layout and content without touching storage or email. It reduces coupling because changes to the email provider only require changes in ReportEmailer. It also clarifies intent through class names, which improves readability for new team members. This change reduces the blast radius of modifications and allows teams to upgrade or replace one area without risking others. It also creates clearer test boundaries: tests for PdfReportGenerator mock only the PDF output, and tests for ReportSaver focus on storage behavior. The correct balance keeps cohesion high in each class and coupling low between classes. Think of dependencies as contracts: each class promises to do one job and requires only the APIs to fulfill it. That explicitness simplifies maintenance and future changes. Maintainability rises because changes are localized: when a requirement evolves, only the class representing that responsibility changes. Testability improves because classes have narrow scope and can be tested without large setup or many mocks. Reusability increases since focused classes like PdfGenerator can be reused by different parts of the system. Readability improves because class names and method lists clearly express intent. Coupling decreases because unrelated dependencies move to the classes that need them. Consider a scenario where the email provider changes: with SRP, only the EmailSender needs modification and tests, rather than multiple classes scattered across the codebase. A misconception is that SRP produces too many tiny classes; the right balance is high cohesion within each class and low coupling across classes. Finally, SRP supports incremental refactoring: small extractions make future changes safer and faster. As you adopt SRP, measure improvement by tracking how often a single change touches multiple classes — that frequency should decrease. Let's consolidate understanding with two assessment questions drawn from the chapter. First, consider a Customer class with getCustomerDetails(), saveCustomerToDatabase(), sendWelcomeEmail(), and validateCustomerAddress(). Which method most clearly violates SRP if the Customer class's role is to represent customer data? The correct selection is sendWelcomeEmail(), because sending email is a distinct communication responsibility that changes independently of data representation. The second question contrasts combining authentication and profile management in a single UserManager. The correct view is that authentication and profile management are distinct responsibilities and should be separated; changes to authentication protocols or session handling are reasons different from profile updates. A common mistake when answering these questions is to equate relatedness with identical reasons to change; two behaviors may seem related but still change for different causes. Keep these three compact ideas in mind as you work with code. First, Single Responsibility Principle: a class should have only one reason to change — group behaviors by their cause, not by method counts. Second, Reason to Change: name the external event that would force a class edit; that naming guides extraction decisions. Third, Cohesion: high cohesion means a class’s methods all serve the single responsibility; aim for high cohesion to make intentions clear. Use these concepts in code reviews: ask whether a planned change would touch multiple concerns and prefer extraction when it would. These three practical reminders help you apply SRP during code review and refactor sessions. First, prefer explicit responsibilities: choose class names that state what will cause a change. Second, keep tests small and focused by extracting side-effecting behavior into dedicated classes. Third, avoid premature abstraction: extract behaviors first, then introduce interfaces when multiple implementations are needed. These rules help maintain balance — you get the benefits of SRP without over-engineering. When you review pull requests, ask: does this change create a new reason to change for the class?
